Agent Acceleration in a Stable Environment

Learning from repeated tasks to make later ones faster and cheaper

  1. Can what an agent learns on earlier tasks lower the time and money of later tasks, with the cost of learning counted?
  2. After how many tasks does the learning pay for itself?
  3. Which parts of the agent should learning change, and should it learn from its own runs or from exploring the environment?
  4. Does what it learned still work on new tasks and after the environment changes, without lowering the success rate?

October 2026

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 01

Problem: make repeated tasks faster and cheaper

An agent runs the same workflow many times with new inputs. What it learns on earlier tasks should lower the time and money of later tasks, with the cost of learning counted, without lowering the success rate.

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 02

How an agent runs a task, and where learning changes it

One attempt is a loop of steps: observe, call the model, act, wait, until the agent stops. Learning across tasks changes the harness around the model to cut steps, model calls and failures; the price is a longer prompt to read.

learning aims to lower it, or to raise successgrows in exchange: learned material is read in the prompta possible direction: a stable prompt prefix is read from the cacheevery symbol: Appendix A0 ↗
ACROSS TASKSrun record→learning, at cost →updated harness: prompt · memory · skills and tools · control code→next task
  • steps in one attempt; one step is one observe–decide–act–wait round (Hua et al., 2025)
  • model calls in step : planner, judge, retries (self-defined)
  • chance that one attempt of agent on task succeeds (Erol et al., 2026)
  • length of the prompt read in step ; learned notes make it longer (Y. Yuan et al., 2026)
  • reading the prompt before writing; input already in the cache is read faster and billed at a lower price (Anthropic, 2026b)

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 03

Example: a web agent that files expense reports

Our running example: a web agent files expense reports; each task is a new report in the same system. Not knowing one rule of the form, that a hotel expense needs check-in and check-out dates, sends the agent into a rework loop.

One hotel report, before the agent knows the rule
WITHOUT LEARNING
The loop is paid again on every hotel report
  • Its extra model calls and seconds are part of , for each of the reports
LEARNING THE RULE ONCE
The rule is learned once, at cost ; later reports skip the loop
  • ; it pays off after reports (page 1)
In this example
  • Environment: the expense system, its forms, the fields each expense type requires, the actions it allows
  • Run record: the steps above, with the error message, and the time and cost of each step
What learning may change here (model weights fixed)
  • Prompt: an instruction read on every call: fill the check-in and check-out dates before submitting a hotel expense
  • Memory: a note read only when relevant: Hotel → check-in and check-out dates required
  • Skill or tool: a procedure the model calls when it needs it: instructions plus a script that fills every field a hotel expense requires
  • Control code: the harness’s own logic, run whatever the model decides: check the required fields before every submit
SCOPEthis example: expense reports on a website→any workflow repeated in one software environment→websites · desktop applications · mobile apps · tool APIs

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 05

Five difficulties, explained (version B)

Cost per task after learning ·
1 · Fewer steps do not always save time
  • A learned hint, or a second model that coaches, adds reading and thinking to every step
  • Steps differ in cost: skipping two clicks saves little if each remaining step waits longer
  • So judge a report by its seconds and dollars, not by its step count
Works: WebCoach (Liu et al., 2025) · ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026) · GenericAgent (Liang et al., 2026)
2 · What can be skipped is known only after a run has succeeded
  • Before the first hotel report goes through, the agent cannot tell the rework from the necessary steps
  • Savings start once a successful run is stored, and storing it costs a full first pass
  • A kind of report never seen before still starts from scratch
Works: EchoPath (Zhao et al., 2026) · MobileGPT (Lee et al., 2024) · ActionEngine (Zhong et al., 2026)
3 · What was learned must help on new tasks and be cheap to read
  • A note learned on hotel reports may not help with meal or travel reports
  • Every note in the prompt is read again on every call; too many notes cost more than they save
  • A misleading note can even lower the success rate
Works: skill and memory modules (Hajimiri et al., 2026) · ClawTrace (Yuan et al., 2026) · SEDM (Xu et al., 2025)
Cost of learning ·
4 · Finding the right change from a failure is costly, and not guaranteed
  • The run record shows that a report was rejected, not whether the prompt, a skill or a check should change
  • Diagnosing, writing a change and re-running tasks all cost model calls
  • The change found can be wrong, fix only some failures, or break other tasks
Works: HarnessFix (Chen et al., 2026) · ESPO (L. Liu et al., 2026) · DRAFT (Qu et al., 2025)
5 · Learning, with its testing, can cost more than the mistakes it removes
  • To trust a change, it must be re-run on many reports, and those runs cost money
  • Without learning, the agent simply pays for its rework on each report
  • Learning pays off only after enough reports: the break-even of page 1
Works: SICA (Robeyns et al., 2025) · ADAS (Hu et al., 2025) · GEA (Weng et al., 2026)

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 06

Five difficulties (version C: diagrams)

Cost per task after learning ·
1 · Fewer steps do not always save time
Each step got longer: judge a report by its seconds, not its steps
Drawn from WebCoach (Liu et al., 2025). Also: ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026), fewer steps, more tokens
2 · Whether a check is needed is not known in advance
Skipping a check saves a step only while the rule still holds
Seen in: DRAFT (Qu et al., 2025), learns tool conditions by trying · SKILL.nb (Hattami et al., 2026), checks before reuse
3 · A trade-off between generalization and cost per use
Seen in: Metis (Dai et al., 2026), keeps both text and code · ActionEngine (Zhong et al., 2026), turns a site map into programs
Cost of learning ·
4 · Finding the cause behind an error message
Each possible cause costs a check; the right one may come late, or never
Seen in: HarnessFix (Chen et al., 2026), finds the faulty step · ESPO (L. Liu et al., 2026), sorts errors first
5 · Learning and testing can cost more than they save
Learning pays off only if enough reports share its cost
Seen in: AI Agents That Matter (Kapoor et al., 2025), late break-even · SICA (Robeyns et al., 2025), large bill, small saving

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 08

How a run record becomes a change, and what the change costs

Every step after reading the run records costs model calls, and these costs are rarely reported next to the savings.

per task ↑ ↓
targeted in exchange unchanged
1 · INPUTRun records, failed and successful, with their time and cost
→
2 · DIAGNOSEFind failures and waste; locate the step and the code responsiblecosts: diagnosis calls
→
3 · PROPOSEA change to one of: prompt · memory · skill or tool · control codecosts: candidate generation
→
4 · RE-TESTOn tasks not used to find the change; old tasks must still passcosts: re-runs of tasks
→
5 · DECIDEKeep the change, or roll it back
IT WORKS
Changes can be found and made automatically, with gains on the final tasks
  • Highest success in five of six settings and 76.0–91.8% fewer model calls at deployment — Growing Harness, BrowseComp-Plus and WebArena-Verified, three models, 50 final tasks per setting, three runs (L. Li et al., 2026)
LEARNING COST LEFT OUT ·
Savings at deployment are usually reported without the learning that produced them
  • 97.4K vs 112.6K tokens and 11.25 vs 14.55 turns per AppWorld task once the memory is frozen; the memory manager’s own calls are not included — Metis (Dai et al., 2026)

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 10

Exploring a site, keeping a checked rule, and using it on the next task

The agent probes the form, writes down what it found together with where it applies and the evidence for it, and reads that note on the next task, so the rework loop of the expense example does not happen.

1 · Explore the form
Change the expense type from Meal to Hotel. Two new required fields appear: check-in and check-out date. Submitting without them returns an error.
2 · Keep a checked rule
site-guide.md
scope: new expense form
IF type = Hotel → check-in and check-out dates required
evidence: 2 probes, 1 error message
re-check: when the form changes
3 · Use it on the next task
New hotel expense + the live page + the saved note → fill every required field → submit once → check the saved report.
WITHOUT THE NOTEsubmit→error→fill the dates→submit again→check
WITH THE NOTEfill the dates→submit→check
REAL CALLS CORRECT THE DESCRIPTION
Trying an action and reading its result can fix what a description gets wrong
  • DRAFT learned from a real call that a tool needs a valid person_id, and wrote it into the tool’s documentation (Qu et al., 2025)
ONE OBSERVATION IS NOT A RULE
A rule written from one observation can be wrong, and a local check can miss it
  • DRAFT generalised from one error message; SkillWeaver’s local checks passed broken functions (Qu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025)

  • Qu, C., Dai, S., Wei, X., et al. (2025). From Exploration to Mastery: Enabling LLMs to Master Tools via Self-Driven Interactions. ICLR 2025 (International Conference on Learning Representations 2025).
  • Zheng, B., Fatemi, M. Y., Jin, X., et al. (2025). SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills. arXiv preprint.
Appendix A9 ↗
AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 11

Across both directions, what learning costs is rarely counted

The learning bill is rarely itemised, proving that a change is correct is the weak link, and a saving measured as fewer steps, or in one setting, does not guarantee less time or money elsewhere.

LEARNING COST ·
Few works count both what learning costs and what it saves
  • 5 of 102 works measured both the seconds or dollars of running tasks and a learning cost: GPTSwarm, MobileGPT, OpenSkill, EchoPath and Unbrowse (initial judgment, calc.) (Zhuge et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Tham et al., 2026)
CORRECTNESS ·
Showing that a change fixed the target without breaking what worked is the open problem
  • In AgentDevel’s ablations, the highest mean score and the fewest regressions on old tasks may have to be traded against each other (Zhang, 2026)
FEWER STEPS ·
Fewer steps is not the same as less time or money
  • Steps 9.7 → 8.3 on WebArena, while total tokens rose 50,847.4 → 53,054.5 in another table whose base set-up is not stated — ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026)
TRANSFER ·
A saving in one setting need not carry over
  • Median cost per task $0.143 vs $0.144 after moving to SkillsBench, no fall — ClawTrace, OpenClaw with gpt-5.4 (Yuan et al., 2026)

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · 12

The closest works save time or money on repeated tasks; none counts the whole loop

In the works we checked, no single result covers all of these at once: any task stream, no training, automatic location of failures and waste, protection of old abilities, every learning and maintenance cost counted, and a net saving over time.

A0 · Page 1’s formulas: the original, ours, and why we changed it

our formulaoriginal formulaoriginal definitionswhat we changed, and why
from the paper
 (Eq. 2)
(Erol et al., 2026)
  • : a model; : a problem
  • : expected dollars of one attempt, input and output tokens times their prices (Eq. 13)
  • : chance that one attempt is correct; attempts are expected until the first correct one, attempts independent
  • becomes the agent: the model plus its harness
  • why: learning changes the harness, not the model
self-defined, adapted
no time formula
(Erol et al., 2026)
  • units per attempt other than dollars, such as time or latency, may matter more (App. D.1)
  • the same form, in seconds
  • why: time and money are reported side by side
  • assumes attempts run one after another
self-defined, adapted
 (Eq. 8)
(Erol et al., 2026)
  • : a dataset of problems; : its empirical distribution, mass on each problem
  • : the lowest cost per success on among the available models
  • the same average over tasks, applied to one agent’s instead of the cheapest model’s; and the same way
  • why: we compare one agent before and after learning
self-defined, adapted
total cost = fixed cost + variable cost (in words)
(Kapoor et al., 2025)

against (Table 2)
(Cai et al., 2024)
  • fixed cost: paid once, to optimise the agent’s design (prompt, hyperparameters)
  • variable cost: paid on every run, set by its input and output tokens
  • : task instances; : one call of the large tool-making model; : one call of the small tool-using model
  • fixed cost ÷ : a cost per task
  • variable part = the average cost per success , so failed attempts are paid for
  • fixed cost widened to exploring, proposing, checking and upkeep — why: our learning does all of these

self-defined
 (Eq. 3)
(Erol et al., 2026)

accuracy and cost optimised jointly (in words)
(Kapoor et al., 2025)
  • : the available models
  • : the lowest cost per success on among them
  • one number becomes a pair, seconds and dollars, lowered together — why: no fixed exchange rate between them
  • learning cost included
  • success floor , fixed in advance — why: an agent must not look cheaper by succeeding less
self-defined
no formula (in words)
(Kapoor et al., 2025)
  • the jointly optimised agent is cheaper in total than the default one after about 1,350 HotPotQA tasks
  • written as a formula by setting — why: computable from measured costs
  • assumes the saving per task stays the same

AGENT ACCELERATION · STABLE ENVIRONMENT · A0 · 2/2

A0 · Every symbol in the agent loop

  • step (one observe–decide–act–wait round); steps in the attempt (Hua et al., 2025)
  • model calls in step (planner, judge, retries …); call index (self-defined)
  • latency of call of step (Li et al., 2026, arXiv · Salesforce Research)
  • time to the first generated token: queueing, sending, prefill of the uncached input (Zhong et al., 2024; Artificial Analysis, 2026)
  • output tokens of the call, thinking included; time per output token after the first (Erol et al., 2026 (adapted); Anthropic, 2026b; Zhong et al., 2024)
  • model time of step ; all its other time (observe, act, wait, harness gaps, back-off) (adapted from Hua et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026, arXiv · Imperial)
  • time hidden because some of it ran at the same time; 0 if strictly serial (Feng et al., 2026, arXiv · UC Berkeley; precedent Kim et al., 2024)
  • tokens the result or screenshot of step adds to the prompt; agent index (Yao et al., 2023; Y. Yuan et al., 2026)
  • length of the prompt step ’s call reads (one call per step); chat template; the call’s output: thinking, message and tool-call tokens (Y. Yuan et al., 2026)
  • input tokens read from the cache, written to it, or uncached (Anthropic, 2026b; Xu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2024)
  • price per token of billing class on serving model (adapted from Erol et al., 2026)
  • billed environment usage (e.g. sandbox hours) (Erol et al., 2026 (adapted))
  • chance that one attempt of agent on task succeeds (Erol et al., 2026)

Time or money of runs — yes: measured seconds or dollars of executing tasks with what was learned; partly: tokens, steps, calls or an author’s estimate only. Learning cost — yes: a measured amount for learning, building or maintaining (tokens, dollars, time, compute or rollouts); partly: an estimate, iteration counts only, or a part knowingly left out. Unseen tasks — yes: tested on tasks that took no part in learning or selection; partly: an online stream that learns as it goes, the same workflow with new parameters, or an unstated split. These are our initial judgments from the cells of the per-work table (calc.), not re-read from the full texts; the representative works on pages 4 and 6 are to be checked one by one before the deck is final.
